extracted.intended_audience: writers and general readers interested in imaginative literature, philosophy of art, and narrative craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing imaginative, 'romantic' prose and philosophical essays that balance wonder and welcome, favor vivid mental pictures over abstract deduction, and avoid narrowness of pure reason or mere novelty. Applicable to fiction and reflective nonfiction interested in moral/aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of the familiar and the unfamiliar (romance)
rubrics_metrics.description: How can we contrive to be at once astonished at the world and yet at home in it? ... It is the purpose of the writer to attempt an explanation ... to set forth my faith as particularly answering this double spiritual need, the need for that mixture of the familiar and the unfamiliar which Christendom has rightly named romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to combine wonder with welcome: present the world so readers feel both astonishment and a sense of being 'at home'. Use narrative and imagery that produce the simultaneous feelings of adventure and security; this balance (romance) is the chief aesthetic aim of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desirability of an active, imaginative life
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing I do not propose to prove ... is this desirability of an active and imaginative life, picturesque and full of a poetical curiosity, a life such as western man at any rate always seems to have desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume and appeal to a reader who values a vivid, curious life. Writing should encourage or exemplify an active imagination—picturesque details, curiosity-driven scenes—rather than anemic or flat description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mental pictures rather than abstract deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: I have attempted in a vague and personal way, in a set of mental pictures rather than in a series of deductions, to state the philosophy in which I have come to believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete images and illustrative anecdotes to long abstract argument when trying to persuade or evoke. Show ideas through scenes and pictures; use individual, autobiographical examples to make philosophical points vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative, autobiographical tone for philosophical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: This book is unavoidably affirmative and therefore unavoidably autobiographical. ... it is an attempt to answer the challenge ... of how he personally has come to believe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting a creed or worldview in essay form, an affirmative, personal tone (autobiographical details, confessions) can make the argument more sincere and persuasive than detached refutation alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere paradox and light sophistry
rubrics_metrics.description: I know nothing so contemptible as a mere paradox; a mere ingenious defence of the indefensible. ... Mere light sophistry is the thing that I happen to despise most of all things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cultivate paradox for its own sake or for cheap cleverness. Ensure paradoxical turns are grounded in genuine insight or truth; avoid flippancy and insincere wit that sacrifices substance for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the protagonist (in fairy-tale/romance) a normal human to achieve wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: The old fairy tale makes the hero a normal human boy; it is his adventures that are startling; they startle him because he is normal. But in the modern psychological novel the hero is abnormal; the centre is not central. Hence the fiercest adventures fail to affect him adequately, and the book is monotonous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stories that aim to elicit wonder, choose an essentially ordinary protagonist who encounters extraordinary situations. Relatability of the hero amplifies the strangeness of events; conversely, making the hero already abnormal risks emotional deadening and monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer imaginative expansion over exhaustive logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is sane because it floats easily in an infinite sea; reason seeks to cross the infinite sea, and so make it finite. The result is mental exhaustion ... The poet only desires exaltation and expansion, a world to stretch himself in. The logician who seeks to get the heavens into his head ... his head that splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creative work, allow expansion, mystery, and multiplicity rather than attempting to reduce everything to a single logical system. Embrace breadth and the sense of the sublime rather than narrowing the world to a closed argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination does not breed insanity; over-reasoning does
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination does not breed insanity. Exactly what does breed insanity is reason. Poets do not go mad; but chess-players do. Mathematicians go mad, and cashiers; but creative artists very seldom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not avoid imaginative or mystical content out of fear that it is psychologically dangerous. The craft of imaginative writing is a healthy expansion; beware of turning narrative into cold analytic systems that risk dulling human feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break monomania by enlarging the world (give air, not arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you were dealing with a mind that was growing morbid, we should be chiefly concerned not so much to give it arguments as to give it air, to convince it that there was something cleaner and cooler outside the suffocation of a single argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story or essay feels narrow or obsessive, introduce broader context, varied characters, or alternative perspectives to release the claustrophobia. In craft terms, avoid a single thin premise stretched to exhaustion; diversify scenes and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of narrow, exhaustive explanatory frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: The thing has shrunk. The deity is less divine than many men; and (according to Haeckel) the whole of life is something much more grey, narrow, and trivial than many separate aspects of it. The parts seem greater than the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing characters, motives, or the world to one explanation (materialism, determinism, single-theme readings). Good writing acknowledges complexity and the 'manifold and even miscellaneous' nature of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor decision, will, or action over endless ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: A man cannot think himself out of mental evil; for it is actually the organ of thought that has become diseased ... Decision is the whole business here; a door must be shut for ever. Every remedy is a desperate remedy. Every cure is a miraculous cure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratively and rhetorically, dramatize decisive acts and moral commitments rather than leaving characters or arguments trapped in perpetual analysis. Plot and moral force often require a voluntaristic turn, not more abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paradox only when it's sincere and truthful
rubrics_metrics.description: I know nothing so contemptible as a mere paradox ... It is as easy as lying; because it is lying. The truth is, of course, that Mr. Shaw is cruelly hampered by the fact that he cannot tell any lie unless he thinks it is the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradox can be powerful when it reveals genuine insight; avoid artificial contradictions meant simply to astonish. Ensure surprising claims are rooted in honest conviction or demonstrable paradoxical truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure argument/essay as riddle and answer (romantic arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is therefore arranged upon the positive principle of a riddle and its answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider framing a philosophical or thematic work by presenting questions, puzzles, or tensions (the riddle) and then resolving them through narrative or reflective 'answers'—this can maintain engagement and dramatize insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of 'originality' that merely rediscovers tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: I did try to be original; and when I had put the last touches to it, I discovered that it was orthodoxy. I only succeeded in inventing all by myself an inferior copy of the existing traditions of civilized religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for genuine originality; test novelty against deeper traditions to avoid producing an 'inferior copy.' Recognize that what feels novel may be longstanding wisdom—examine whether innovation truly adds value.
